title: Snapshot Array
statement:
Design a `SnapshotArray`: an integer array of a given `length` whose elements all start at `0`, and which can record snapshots of itself.

It supports three operations:

- `set i v`: set the element at index `i` to the value `v`.
- `snap`: take a snapshot of the whole array and return its **snapshot id**. Snapshot ids are consecutive integers starting from `0`, so the first snapshot has id `0`, the next `1`, and so on.
- `get i s`: return the value that the element at index `i` had at the moment snapshot `s` was taken. Changes made after that snapshot do not affect the answer.

Read the operations from the input, process them in order, and print the result of every `snap` and every `get` operation (`set` prints nothing).

The array can be huge and snapshots are frequent, so copying the whole array on every `snap` is too slow and uses too much memory.
input_format:
The first line contains two integers `length` and `q`, the array length and the number of operations.
Each of the next `q` lines is one operation: `set i v`, `snap` or `get i s`.
output_format: For every `snap` and `get` operation, in order, print one line with its result (the snapshot id for `snap`, the value for `get`).
constraints: In every `get i s`, snapshot `s` has already been taken (0 ≤ s < number of `snap` operations so far)

examples.input:
3 7
set 0 5
snap
set 0 6
get 0 0
snap
get 0 1
get 1 1
examples.explanation: Index 0 is set to 5 and snapshot 0 is taken. Setting it to 6 afterwards does not change snapshot 0, so `get 0 0` is 5. Snapshot 1 sees 6. Index 1 was never set, so it is still 0.

examples.input:
2 8
set 1 4
set 1 9
snap
set 1 2
get 1 0
snap
get 1 1
get 0 0
examples.explanation: Two sets before the first snapshot: only the last one (9) is visible in snapshot 0. After the next set the second snapshot sees 2. Index 0 was never written, so it is 0.

complexity.time: O(1) for set and snap, O(log q) for get

hints: A snapshot does not need to copy the array. Most elements do not change between two snapshots, so only record changes.

For every index keep a list of (snapshot id at the time of the write, value) pairs, in increasing order of snapshot id. A second `set` on the same index within the same snapshot just overwrites the last pair.
To answer `get i s`, binary search that index's list for the last entry whose snapshot id is at most `s`. If there is none, the value is still the initial 0.
brute:
import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
length, q = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
arr = [0] * length
snaps = []
out = []
p = 2
for _ in range(q):
    op = data[p]
    if op == 'set':
        arr[int(data[p + 1])] = int(data[p + 2])
        p += 3
    elif op == 'snap':
        p += 1
        snaps.append(arr[:])
        out.append(len(snaps) - 1)
    else:
        out.append(snaps[int(data[p + 2])][int(data[p + 1])])
        p += 3
print('\n'.join(map(str, out)))
